tool.name: Vue
tool.tagline: Progressive JavaScript framework with fine-grained reactivity and single-file components
tool.description: Vue is a JavaScript framework for building user interfaces from components whose templates update automatically when reactive state changes. It scales from a sprinkle of interactivity on a page to full single-page apps with Vue Router and Pinia, and to server-rendered sites with Nuxt. Vue 3 centres on the Composition API, `<script setup>` single-file components and a Proxy-based reactivity system.

glossary.def: A reusable piece of a Vue screen, such as a button, a card or a whole page, with its own markup, logic and styles. Components can contain other components.
How components nest inside each other, like a family tree: the App component contains a header and a list, the list contains items, and so on.
A .vue file that holds one component: its logic in <script setup>, its markup in <template> and its CSS in <style>.
In Vue, the HTML-like markup of a component, in its <template> block, with placeholders such as {{ name }} and special v- attributes that Vue fills in and keeps up to date from your data.
A special attribute in a Vue template whose name starts with v-, such as v-if or v-for, that tells Vue to do something with the element based on a JavaScript expression.
Vue's system for noticing when data changes and automatically updating everything that used that data, such as the page or a computed value.
In Vue, a reactive box made with ref(value). You read and change its contents through .value in script code; templates unwrap it for you.
A value made with computed() that Vue works out from other reactive data, remembers, and recalculates only when that data changes.
In Vue's reactivity, a reactive value that some code (a template, computed or watcher) read, so Vue re-runs that code when it changes. In a project, a package it needs.
Vue mounts a component when it creates its elements and puts them on the page, and unmounts it when it removes them.
A popular build tool for web apps: while you work it runs your app on your own computer and updates it as you save; for publishing it bundles your code into finished files.
The package manager that comes with Node.js: the command you use to download JavaScript packages into a project and to run the project's commands, as in npm run dev.
JavaScript with type labels added, such as name: string, that a checker reads to catch mistakes before the code runs. It is turned into plain JavaScript to run.
A browser extension for inspecting Vue apps: it shows the component tree, each component's data, events and Pinia stores, and a performance timeline.
Vue's style of writing component logic as ordinary functions such as ref(), computed() and onMounted(), usually inside <script setup>. It replaced the older Options API.
Vue's older style of writing a component as an object with sections like data, methods and computed. It still works, but new code usually uses the Composition API.
The inputs a component receives from the component that uses it, written like HTML attributes (<TodoItem :done="true" />). The child may read them but not change them.
A function-like helper such as defineProps that you don't import, because Vue's build step reads it and replaces it with real code before the browser runs anything.
A link where a form field shows a value from your data and typing into the field updates that data, in both directions at once. Vue's v-model creates one.
To send a named event from a child component up to its parent, optionally with data, as in emit('rename', newName). The parent listens with @rename.
A placeholder, <slot />, in a component's template where the parent's own markup is inserted. Named slots allow several; scoped slots also hand data from the child to that markup.
Code registered with watch() or watchEffect() that Vue runs whenever certain reactive data changes, used for side effects such as fetching or saving.
A function such as onMounted or onUnmounted that Vue calls at a set moment in a component's life: after it appears on the page, after it updates, before it is removed.
A ref="name" attribute in a template plus useTemplateRef('name') in script, giving your code the actual page element (or child component) once it is on the page.
A function named useSomething that packages reusable logic made of refs, computed properties, watchers and lifecycle hooks, so several components can share it.
Vue's way for a component to make a value available (provide) to every component below it, however deep, which they read with inject instead of receiving props at each level.
Passing props down through several layers of components that don't use them, only so a deeply nested component can get them.
Vue's official store library: it keeps app-wide state, such as the signed-in user or a cart, in one shared place (a store) any component can use.
Vue's official router: it decides which page component to show for the current URL and lets users move between pages without reloading.
Choosing what to show based on the URL. In a Vue app, a router picks which page component to display for the current address; on a server, it picks which code handles a request.
A function Vue Router calls before moving to another page, which can allow the move, cancel it or send the user somewhere else, such as to a login page.
Breaking an app's JavaScript into several smaller files so the browser downloads each part only when it is needed, instead of everything up front.
In JavaScript, a stand-in object (made with new Proxy) that wraps a real object and lets code step in whenever a property is read or changed. Vue's reactive() is built on proxies.
In Vue, one round of updates: Vue collects state changes and updates the page for all of them together a moment later; await nextTick() waits until that has happened.
A built-in Vue component, <Teleport to="body">, that puts its content somewhere else on the page while it still behaves as part of its component.
A built-in Vue component that keeps a component's state when it is switched out (for example on another tab) instead of destroying it.
Your own v- attribute, defined as an object of lifecycle hooks that receive the element, for low-level page tricks like focusing an input.
In Vue's reactivity, a function that Vue runs while recording which reactive values it reads, and re-runs when any of them change. Renders, computed properties and watchers are effects.

A lightweight copy of the page's structure kept as plain JavaScript objects (vnodes). Vue builds a new one on each update, compares it with the old one and changes the real page only where they differ.
A JavaScript function that returns the virtual DOM tree for a component. Vue turns every template into one; you can also write them by hand with h().
The step where Vue in the browser takes over HTML that was produced on the server, attaching event listeners and reactivity so the page becomes interactive.
An error where the browser's first render produces different output from the HTML the server sent, so Vue can't simply take it over.
A framework built on Vue that adds server rendering, file-based pages, data loading and server code, ready to use.
Drawing only the rows of a long list that are currently visible on screen, and swapping them as the user scrolls, instead of creating thousands of elements.
Waiting until something has stopped changing for a short moment before reacting, such as searching only once the user pauses typing.
A small storage area the browser keeps for each website, holding text under names you choose. It survives reloading the page and restarting the browser.

concepts.name: Creating a Vue app
concepts.summary: Learn what Vue is, create a project with Vite, see what a .vue component file holds, and start the app on a page.
concepts.why: Every Vue project starts the same way, and knowing what each generated file does makes the rest of the tools unsurprising.
concepts.body:
Changing a page by hand, element by element, gets out of control in a big app: the page easily stops matching your data. **Vue** fixes this: you describe what the page should show for your data, and when the data changes, Vue updates the page for you.

Vue is a **framework**: a bigger toolkit that sets the structure of your app, where you fill in the parts and Vue decides when to run them. You build the **user interface** (UI), meaning the screens, buttons and forms people use, out of **components**: reusable pieces such as a button, a card or a whole page.

Vue can be dropped into one existing page, but most projects are whole apps. You create one with **npm**, the **package manager** that comes with Node.js. It downloads **packages**: code others have published under a name, like `vue`. In a terminal:

```bash
npm create vue@latest my-app
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev
```

The first command asks a few questions (answer No to the extras for now). `npm run dev` starts **Vite**, the **build tool** Vue uses to prepare your code for the browser: it runs your app on your own computer at an address like `http://localhost:5173` and updates the page as soon as you save a file.

Each component lives in a **single-file component** (SFC): a `.vue` file with up to three blocks:

- `<script setup>`: the component's JavaScript. Every variable, function and import at its top level can be used in the template.
- `<template>`: the component's HTML. A Vue **template** is HTML with extras, such as `{{ name }}` to show a value; the next lessons cover them.
- `<style scoped>`: CSS that applies only to this component's elements.

Browsers can't read `.vue` files, so Vite translates each one into plain JavaScript before sending it.

The file `src/main.js` starts the app. It creates the app from your top component and **mounts** it, meaning Vue draws it inside an element of `index.html`:

```js
createApp(App).mount('#app')
```

`createApp` returns an **app instance**. Before mounting, you add app-wide extras to it, such as page navigation with `app.use(router)`; these add-ons are called **plugins**.

Install the **Vue DevTools** browser extension early: it shows your components and their data, which saves a lot of `console.log` hunting.
takeaways: `npm create vue@latest` creates a Vue project; `npm run dev` runs it on your computer
A `.vue` file has `<script setup>`, `<template>` and `<style scoped>` blocks
`createApp(App).mount('#app')` starts the app; add plugins before mounting
pitfalls: Calling `app.use(...)` after `mount()`; plugins must be added before the app is mounted.

quiz.q: In a `<script setup>` block, which variables can the template use?
options: Only those listed in a `return` statement
Every top-level variable and function, including imports
quiz.explain: `<script setup>` makes every top-level variable, function and import available to the template automatically.

concepts.name: Template syntax and v-bind
concepts.summary: Show data in templates with {{ }}, set attributes from data with v-bind (:), and learn what a directive is.
concepts.why: Templates are where most Vue code lives; reading and writing them fluently is the first real Vue skill.
concepts.body:
A Vue template is ordinary HTML with a few additions. To show a value as text, put it in double curly braces: `{{ user.name }}`. Vue shows it as plain text, never as HTML, so text a user typed can't sneak code into your page (the XSS attack from the DOM lesson).

Inside `{{ }}` and directive values you write **JavaScript expressions**, not statements: `{{ price * qty }}`, `{{ ok ? 'Yes' : 'No' }}` and `{{ formatDate(d) }}` work; `if` blocks and variable declarations do not.

Special attributes that start with `v-` are called **directives**: each tells Vue to do something with the element, based on a JavaScript expression, and Vue re-evaluates that expression whenever the data it reads changes.

`{{ }}` doesn't work inside attributes. To set an attribute from your data, use the **`v-bind`** directive, almost always written as just `:`:

- `:src="avatarUrl"`, `:disabled="isSaving"` — a `false`, `null` or `undefined` boolean value removes the attribute.
- `:id` alone (same-name shorthand, Vue 3.4+) means `:id="id"`.
- `v-bind="attrsObject"` spreads an object of attributes.
- `:[attrName]="value"` binds a dynamic attribute name.

`:class` and `:style` are special: they accept objects and arrays, so `:class="{ active: isActive, 'text-danger': hasError }"` toggles classes and merges with a static `class` attribute.

You will meet the directives `v-if`, `v-for`, `v-on` and `v-model` next. `v-html` inserts raw HTML: use it only with content you trust.
takeaways: `{{ expr }}` shows a value as plain text; directives take JavaScript expressions
`:attr="expr"` is shorthand for `v-bind:attr`; falsy booleans remove the attribute
`:class` and `:style` accept objects and arrays
pitfalls: Writing `src="{{ url }}"`; attributes need `:src="url"`, mustaches only work in text.

quiz.q: Which binding correctly sets an image's src from the `url` variable?
quiz.explain: Attributes are bound with v-bind, written `:src`; mustache syntax only works in text content.

concepts.name: Reactive state: ref and reactive
concepts.summary: Declare reactive state with ref() and reactive(), know when .value is needed, and see why destructuring can break the link.
concepts.why: Reactive state is what makes the page update itself; mixing up ref and reactive causes most beginner bugs.
concepts.body:
Ordinary variables don't update the page when they change. For data that should, Vue gives you **reactive state**: values Vue watches, so that when one changes, Vue redraws (**re-renders**) every component that used it. This automatic updating is called **reactivity**. You create reactive state with two functions.

**`ref(value)`** wraps any value (number, string, object, array) in a small object, a **ref**, with a `.value` property. In `<script>` you read and write `count.value`; in the template Vue unwraps refs for you, so you write `{{ count }}`. Objects inside a ref are made reactive all the way down, so `todos.value.push(x)` updates the page too.

**`reactive(object)`** makes the object itself reactive, with no `.value`: `state.count++`. It returns a **proxy**: a stand-in that looks like your object but lets Vue notice every read and change. It has limits:

- It only works with objects, arrays, Maps and Sets, not single values like numbers or strings.
- You cannot replace the whole object (`state = reactive({...})` disconnects the template from the old one).
- Destructuring (`const { count } = state`) copies plain values and loses reactivity; use `toRefs(state)` if you need that.

Because of these limits the Vue docs recommend **`ref` as the default** way to declare state, and many teams use `ref` exclusively.

Vue doesn't update the page the instant you change state. It collects all the changes made together and updates each component once, a moment later; this grouping is called **batching**. If your code needs the updated page right after a change, wait with `await nextTick()`.

A ref nested in a reactive object is unwrapped on access, but refs inside arrays and Maps are not.
concepts.code:
import { ref, reactive, toRefs, nextTick } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
count.value++
console.log(count.value)            // 1

const todos = ref([])
todos.value.push({ text: 'learn Vue' })   // deep: this is reactive too

const state = reactive({ user: 'Ada', visits: 1 })
state.visits++                      // no .value with reactive

const { visits } = state            // plain number, NOT reactive
const { user } = toRefs(state)      // user is a ref linked to state.user
state.user = 'Grace'
console.log(visits, user.value)     // 2 'Grace'

const box = reactive({ n: ref(1) })
console.log(box.n)                  // 1 (ref unwrapped inside reactive)

await nextTick()                    // DOM now reflects the changes
takeaways: `ref()` for any value, used via `.value` in `<script>` and unwrapped in templates
`reactive()` makes an object reactive through a proxy; don't reassign or destructure it
Updates are batched; `await nextTick()` to see the updated page
pitfalls: Forgetting `.value` in `<script>`: `if (count > 3)` compares the ref object, not the number.
Destructuring a reactive object and expecting the copies to stay reactive.

quiz.q: `const state = reactive({ n: 1 }); let { n } = state; state.n = 5;` What is `n` now?
quiz.explain: Destructuring copies the current plain number (1); the local variable is not connected to the proxy.

quiz.q: Why do the Vue docs recommend ref() as the main way to declare state?
options: It is faster than reactive in every case
It works with any value type and can be reassigned or passed around without losing reactivity
quiz.explain: reactive() only takes objects and breaks on reassignment or destructuring; ref() avoids both limitations.

concepts.name: Computed properties
concepts.summary: Derive values from reactive state with computed(), which remembers the result until the data it uses changes.
concepts.why: Derived values belong in computed properties, not in duplicated state or slow template expressions.
concepts.body:
A **computed property** works out a value from other reactive state:

```js
const remaining = computed(() => todos.value.filter(t => !t.done).length)
```

`computed()` returns a read-only ref, so in `<script>` you read `remaining.value` and in the template simply `{{ remaining }}`.

Two features make computeds better than calling a function in the template:

- **Dependency tracking**: Vue records which reactive values your function read (its **dependencies**) and recalculates only when one of them changes.
- **Caching**: reading it again returns the remembered result; a plain function called in the template would re-run every time the component re-renders.

Keep the function **pure**: it should only calculate and return a value, without fetching, changing other state or touching the page. Side effects belong in watchers (a later lesson). Also never change the computed result itself (for example by sorting it in place); treat it as read-only.

For the rare two-way case, pass `get` and `set` to make a **writable computed**, for example a `fullName` that splits back into first and last names.

Since Vue 3.4 a computed only tells the code using it to update when its value actually changes, so `const isEven = computed(() => n.value % 2 === 0)` does not re-render consumers when `n` goes from 2 to 4.

A common mistake is copying derived data into a separate `ref` and updating it by hand. If a value can be computed from existing state, make it a computed.
takeaways: `computed(() => ...)` returns a cached, read-only ref
It recomputes only when a reactive dependency changes
Keep the function pure; use get/set only when two-way derivation is needed
pitfalls: Changing data inside the computed's function, such as `list.value.sort()`, which sorts the original state.

quiz.q: A template shows `{{ total }}` three times, where total is a computed over a large array. How many times does the computed's function run per render if nothing changed?
options: Zero; the cached value is reused
quiz.explain: Computeds are cached until a dependency changes, so unchanged state means no re-evaluation.

concepts.name: Conditionals and lists
concepts.summary: Show or hide elements with v-if / v-show, and repeat them for each item with v-for and a stable :key.
concepts.why: Almost every screen shows or hides things and repeats things; getting keys right prevents subtle UI bugs.
concepts.body:
**`v-if`**, `v-else-if` and `v-else` add or remove elements entirely. To toggle a group without a wrapper element, put `v-if` on a `<template>` tag, which renders nothing itself.

**`v-show`** keeps the element and toggles CSS `display`. Prefer it for things toggled very often (cheap to switch); prefer `v-if` when the condition rarely changes or the content is expensive (it is not rendered at all while false).

**`v-for`** repeats an element for each item:

- Arrays: `v-for="(item, index) in items"`.
- Objects: `v-for="(value, key) in obj"`.
- Ranges: `v-for="n in 5"` gives 1 to 5.

Always give list items a **`:key`** with a stable, unique id (`:key="todo.id"`). Vue uses keys to match old and new elements when the list changes. Without them, or with the array index as key, Vue reuses elements by position, so what's inside items (typed text, component state, focus) can end up attached to the wrong row after inserting, removing or sorting.

Don't put `v-if` and `v-for` on the same element. In Vue 3 `v-if` is evaluated first and cannot see the loop variable. Filter in a computed instead, or wrap with `<template v-for>` and put the `v-if` inside.
takeaways: `v-if` adds/removes elements; `v-show` toggles CSS display
`v-for` needs a stable unique `:key`, not the index, for dynamic lists
Filter with a computed instead of combining v-if and v-for
pitfalls: Using the index as key in a list that can be reordered or have items removed.

quiz.q: A list of inputs uses `:key="index"`. You delete the first item. What can go wrong?
options: Typed text can shift to the wrong row because elements are reused by position
Vue throws a duplicate key error
quiz.explain: With index keys, the element at position 0 is reused for what was item 1, so typed text stays attached to the wrong data.

concepts.name: Event handling
concepts.summary: Listen to DOM events with v-on (@), call handlers with arguments, and use event and key modifiers.
concepts.why: User interaction drives every app; Vue's modifiers remove most repetitive event code.
concepts.body:
**`v-on`**, shortened to `@`, attaches a listener: `@click="handler"`. The value can be:

- A **method name**: `@click="save"` calls `save(event)` with the browser's event object.
- An **inline statement**: `@click="count++"` or `@click="remove(item.id)"`. If you also need the event, pass the special `$event` variable: `@click="remove(item.id, $event)"`.

**Event modifiers** are suffixes that handle common chores for you:

- `.prevent` calls `preventDefault()`, e.g. `@submit.prevent="onSubmit"` stops the page reload.
- `.stop` stops propagation; `.self` fires only if the event target is the element itself.
- `.once` removes the listener after the first call; `.passive` promises you won't call `preventDefault()`, which keeps scrolling smooth; `.capture` runs the handler on the event's way down, before inner elements see it.

**Key modifiers** filter keyboard events: `@keyup.enter="send"`, `@keydown.esc="close"`, and combinations with system keys like `@keyup.ctrl.enter`. Add `.exact` to require exactly those modifiers. Mouse buttons have `.left`, `.right` and `.middle`.

Handlers are functions declared in `<script setup>`. Keep template statements short; once a handler does more than one thing, move it into a function. Vue removes template listeners automatically when the component is removed from the page, so you never clean them up yourself (only listeners you add manually with `addEventListener`).
takeaways: `@event="method"` or an inline statement; use `$event` for the event object
`.prevent`, `.stop`, `.once`, `.self` replace manual event-object calls
Key modifiers like `@keyup.enter` filter keyboard events
pitfalls: Forgetting `.prevent` on a form's submit so the browser reloads the page.

quiz.q: What does `@submit.prevent="save"` do?
options: Stops the event from bubbling only
Prevents save from being called twice
quiz.explain: The .prevent modifier calls preventDefault (stopping navigation) before invoking the handler.

concepts.name: Form input bindings with v-model
concepts.summary: Connect form fields to state with v-model on text inputs, checkboxes, radio buttons and selects.
concepts.why: Forms are everywhere, and v-model saves writing a value binding plus a listener for every input.
concepts.body:
**`v-model`** creates a **two-way binding** between a form element and a ref: the element shows the ref's value, and typing updates the ref. It is a shortcut for a value binding plus an event listener, chosen per element type:

- `<input>` and `<textarea>`: binds `value` and listens to `input`.
- Checkbox: binds `checked` (a boolean). Several checkboxes bound to the same **array** collect the `value`s of the checked ones.
- Radio: the ref holds the `value` of the selected radio.
- `<select>`: the ref holds the selected option's value, or an array with `multiple`.

Modifiers adjust the behaviour:

- `.trim` removes spaces at the start and end.
- `.number` casts the input to a number (when it parses).
- `.lazy` updates on `change` (when the user leaves the input) instead of on every keystroke.

`v-model` ignores any initial `value`, `checked` or `selected` attributes in the template: the JavaScript state is the single **source of truth**, so set initial values in the ref.

Option values do not have to be strings: bind `:value="obj"` on options or checkboxes and the model receives the object itself.

To check what users typed (**validation**), keep it simple at first: a computed `errors` object built from the inputs, and a submit handler that checks it. Larger forms usually use a **library**, ready-made code from someone else, such as VeeValidate or FormKit. Later you'll make your own components work with `v-model` too.
takeaways: `v-model` = value binding + input listener, adapted to each input type
Several checkboxes on one array ref collect the checked values
`.trim`, `.number` and `.lazy` modify the binding; initial values live in the ref
pitfalls: Setting `value="..."` or `checked` in the template and expecting it to be the initial state; v-model ignores it.

quiz.q: Three checkboxes with values 'a', 'b', 'c' all use v-model="picked" where picked = ref([]). The user checks a and c. What is picked.value?
quiz.explain: When bound to an array, checkboxes add and remove their value in that array.

concepts.name: Components and props
concepts.summary: Split the page into components, import and use them, and pass data down with defineProps.
concepts.why: Components are Vue's unit of reuse and organisation; props are how parents configure them.
concepts.body:
Each `.vue` file is a component. To use one, import it in `<script setup>` and write it as a tag, by convention in PascalCase (every word capitalised): `<TodoItem />`. No registration step is needed.

A component declares the data it accepts from its parent with **props**, using `defineProps`. It is a **compiler macro**: you don't import it, because Vue's build step replaces it with real code:

```js
const props = defineProps({
  title: { type: String, required: true },
  count: { type: Number, default: 0 },
})
```

With **TypeScript** (JavaScript plus type labels, covered at the Advanced level) you can write `defineProps<{ title: string; count?: number }>()` instead. Since Vue 3.5, destructuring props is reactive and is the usual way to give defaults: `const { title, count = 0 } = defineProps(...)`. Vue's build step rewrites `count` to `props.count`, so it stays reactive.

The parent passes props as attributes: static `title="Inbox"` or bound `:count="unread"` (without the colon, `count="3"` is the string "3"). Props declared in camelCase can be written kebab-case in templates (`:max-items`).

Props follow **one-way data flow**: when the parent's value changes the child updates, but the child must never assign to a prop. Vue warns if you try. If the child needs a local, editable copy, initialise a ref from the prop; if it wants to change the parent's data, it emits an event (next lesson).
takeaways: Import a component in `<script setup>` and use it as a PascalCase tag
`defineProps` declares inputs; destructure with defaults in Vue 3.5+
Data flows down one way: never assign to a prop
pitfalls: Passing `count="3"` without the colon, which sends the string "3" rather than a number.

quiz.q: A child component wants to change a value it received as a prop from its parent. What is the correct approach?
options: Make the prop a reactive() object and mutate its fields
Emit an event so the parent updates its own state
Use v-if to re-create the parent
quiz.explain: Props are read-only in the child; the owner of the data (the parent) changes it in response to an event.

concepts.name: Component events with defineEmits
concepts.summary: Let children notify parents by declaring and emitting custom events.
concepts.why: Events are the other half of the component contract: props go down, events go up.
concepts.body:
A child talks back to its parent by **emitting** (sending) events. Declare them with the `defineEmits` compiler macro, which returns an `emit` function:

```js
const emit = defineEmits(['remove', 'rename'])
emit('rename', newName)
```

The parent listens exactly like a DOM event: `<TodoItem @remove="deleteTodo(todo.id)" @rename="(name) => todo.name = name" />`. Extra arguments passed to `emit` become the handler's arguments. Events emitted in camelCase (`emit('itemSelected')`) can be listened to as `@item-selected`.

In the template you can emit directly with `$emit('remove')`.

With TypeScript, describe the data each event carries (its payload) like this:

```ts
const emit = defineEmits<{ rename: [name: string]; remove: [] }>()
```

Declaring events is not just documentation. If the parent listens for an event the child **didn't declare**, Vue attaches that listener to the child's outermost element as an ordinary browser listener, which can make a `click` fire twice. Declared events also show up in Vue DevTools.

Component events **do not bubble**: only the direct parent can listen. For distant components use provide/inject or a Pinia store (both covered soon) instead of passing events up through many layers.

A useful convention: name events after what happened (`select`, `close`, `update:modelValue`), not after what the parent should do.
takeaways: `const emit = defineEmits([...])`, then `emit('name', payload)`
Parents listen with `@name`; payload arguments go to the handler
Component events don't bubble; declare all emitted events
pitfalls: Emitting an undeclared `click` event while the root element also fires a native click, so the parent handler runs twice.

quiz.q: A grandchild emits 'save'. Can the grandparent listen with @save on the parent component?
options: No, only the direct parent receives component events
Only if the event name is kebab-case
Yes, component events bubble like DOM events
quiz.explain: Vue component events do not bubble; the middle component would need to re-emit or you use provide/inject or a store.

concepts.name: v-model on components (defineModel)
concepts.summary: Make your own components work with v-model using defineModel, including named and multiple models.
concepts.why: Reusable inputs, toggles and pickers should feel like native inputs to the parent.
concepts.body:
On a component, `v-model="query"` expands to a prop plus an event: `:modelValue="query"` and `@update:modelValue="v => query = v"`. Since Vue 3.4 the **`defineModel()`** compiler macro implements both sides for you:

```js
const model = defineModel()          // a ref synced with the parent
model.value = 'new'                  // emits update:modelValue
```

The returned ref reads the parent's prop and, when you assign to it, emits the update event. You can bind it straight to a native input: `<input v-model="model">`.

Options mirror props: `defineModel({ type: Number, default: 0, required: true })`, or typed with `defineModel<number>()`.

Components can expose **several models** by name. The parent writes `v-model:title="t"` and `v-model:done="d"`, and the child declares `defineModel('title')` and `defineModel('done')`.

Custom **modifiers** are supported: the parent writes `v-model.capitalize="text"` and the child destructures `const [model, modifiers] = defineModel({ set(v) { return modifiers.capitalize ? cap(v) : v } })`.

One subtlety: if the parent does not pass a value, `defineModel` keeps a local value so the component still works on its own. If you give a `default` and the parent passes nothing, the parent's ref and the child can show different values, so prefer requiring the model or matching defaults on both sides.
takeaways: `v-model` on a component = `modelValue` prop + `update:modelValue` event
`defineModel()` returns a ref that emits updates when assigned
Use named models (`v-model:title`) for several bindings on one component
pitfalls: Mutating the parent's object via `model.value.field = x`; that bypasses the update event. Assign a new object instead.

quiz.q: Inside a child, `const m = defineModel()` and the code runs `m.value = 5`. What happens?
options: Only the child's local copy changes
Vue warns that props are read-only
The child emits update:modelValue with 5 and the parent's bound ref becomes 5
quiz.explain: defineModel's ref emits the update event on assignment; the parent's v-model listener writes the value.

concepts.name: Slots and scoped slots
concepts.summary: Pass template content into components with default, named and scoped slots.
concepts.why: Slots let one component control layout or behaviour while the parent controls the markup: the basis of layouts, cards, tables and lists.
concepts.body:
Props pass data; **slots** pass template content. A component marks where content goes with `<slot />`; whatever the parent writes between the component's tags is rendered there. Content inside `<slot>` itself is the **fallback** shown when the parent passes nothing.

**Named slots** allow several insertion points. The child writes `<slot name="header" />` and the parent targets it with `<template #header>...</template>` (`#` is short for `v-slot:`). Content outside any `<template #...>` goes to the default slot.

Slot content belongs to the **parent**: it sees the parent's variables, not the child's. When the child needs to give data to the slot, use a **scoped slot**: the child binds props on the slot, `<slot name="item" :item="row" :index="i" />`, and the parent receives them, typically destructured: `<template #item="{ item, index }">`.

Scoped slots allow "renderless" components: the child owns the logic (fetching, splitting results into pages, selection) and the parent decides exactly how each piece looks.

Inside the child, `useSlots()` (or `$slots` in the template) tells you which slots were provided, which is handy for omitting a wrapper: `<header v-if="$slots.header">`. With TypeScript, `defineSlots<{ item(props: { item: Row }): any }>()` types the slot props.
takeaways: `<slot />` renders the parent's content; inner content is the fallback
Named slots: `<slot name="x">` in the child, `<template #x>` in the parent
Scoped slots pass child data up: `<template #item="{ item }">`
pitfalls: Expecting slot content to read the child's variables; it only sees the parent's scope unless passed as slot props.

quiz.q: A child renders `<slot :user="currentUser" />`. How does the parent read currentUser in its default slot content?
options: With `<template #default="{ user }">` (or v-slot on the component)
quiz.explain: Slot props are received through v-slot (# shorthand) and can be destructured.

concepts.name: Watchers and side effects
concepts.summary: Run side effects when state changes with watch and watchEffect, and cancel async work that has become out of date.
concepts.why: Fetching when an input changes, saving to localStorage (the browser's small per-site storage) and working with non-Vue code all need watchers.
concepts.body:
Computeds derive values; **watchers** run side effects in response to changes.

**`watch(source, callback, options)`** watches an explicit source: a ref, a reactive object, a getter function, or an array of these. The callback receives `(newValue, oldValue, onCleanup)`.

- To watch a property of a reactive object or a destructured prop, pass a getter: `watch(() => props.id, ...)` or `watch(() => id, ...)`. Passing `state.count` directly passes a plain number and does not work.
- `{ immediate: true }` runs the callback once right away; `{ once: true }` runs it only on the first change.
- Watching a reactive object watches every nested property automatically; for a ref holding an object, add `{ deep: true }` (or a number to limit depth).

**`watchEffect(fn)`** runs immediately and re-runs whenever any reactive value it read changes, with no explicit source list. It is concise, but it's less obvious what it depends on, and only values read before the first `await` are tracked.

Async watchers must handle **out-of-date results**: if the id changes twice quickly, the first request may finish last. Vue 3.5 adds `onWatcherCleanup(fn)`, called before the next run and on stop; use it to abort the old request.

By default callbacks run before the component updates; use `{ flush: 'post' }` (or `watchPostEffect`) to see the updated page. Watchers created at the top level of `<script setup>` stop automatically when the component is removed; both functions also return a stop function for manual control.
takeaways: `watch(source, cb)` for explicit sources; use a getter for reactive properties and props
`watchEffect` tracks whatever it reads before any `await` and runs immediately
Cancel out-of-date async work with `onWatcherCleanup` (3.5+) or the onCleanup argument
pitfalls: `watch(state.count, ...)` passes a number, not a source; use `watch(() => state.count, ...)`.
Using a watcher to copy derived data into another ref instead of a computed.

quiz.q: Which correctly watches the `id` prop destructured with `const { id } = defineProps(...)`?
quiz.explain: A destructured prop is compiled to props.id, a property access, so it must be wrapped in a getter to be watched.

concepts.name: Lifecycle hooks and template refs
concepts.summary: Run code when a component mounts or unmounts and get direct access to DOM elements with useTemplateRef.
concepts.why: Working with charts, maps, focus and widgets from other libraries needs the actual page element and the right moment.
concepts.body:
Each component goes through a **lifecycle**, and **lifecycle hooks** let you run code at each stage: setup runs, the component is mounted into the DOM, it updates when state changes, and finally it unmounts. Register callbacks with:

- `onMounted(fn)` — the DOM exists; start up other libraries, measure elements, add global listeners.
- `onUpdated(fn)` — after a re-render caused by state change (rarely needed).
- `onUnmounted(fn)` — clean up: remove listeners, clear timers, destroy library instances.
- `onBeforeMount`, `onBeforeUpdate`, `onBeforeUnmount` and `onErrorCaptured` exist for finer control.

These must be called **while `<script setup>` first runs**, not inside a `setTimeout` or after an `await`, because Vue attaches them to the component currently being created.

If the page is first rendered on a server (covered at Expert level), only the setup code runs there; mounted hooks run only in the browser, so browser-only code belongs in `onMounted`.

To reach a DOM element, add a `ref` attribute in the template and read it with **`useTemplateRef`** (Vue 3.5+). This is a **template ref**:

```js
const input = useTemplateRef('search')   // <input ref="search">
onMounted(() => input.value.focus())
```

The ref is `null` until mount and after unmount. On a component tag, the ref gives the component instance, but with `<script setup>` only what the child exposes via `defineExpose({ ... })` is accessible. Use them sparingly: most things are better done by changing state and letting the template follow.
takeaways: `onMounted` for DOM work; `onUnmounted` to clean up
Register hooks while setup first runs, never after an await
`useTemplateRef('name')` + `ref="name"` gives the element; null before mount
pitfalls: Reading a template ref at the top of `<script setup>`; the element doesn't exist until mounted.

quiz.q: Why might `onMounted` registered after `await fetchConfig()` in setup never run?
options: Lifecycle hooks must be registered synchronously while setup is running
await is not allowed in script setup
quiz.explain: After an await, Vue no longer knows which component is being set up, so the hook can't be bound to it.

concepts.name: Composables
concepts.summary: Move reusable logic built from refs, computeds, watchers and lifecycle hooks into your own useXxx() functions.
concepts.why: Composables are the main way to reuse logic in modern Vue, replacing the older 'mixins'.
concepts.body:
A **composable** is a function that packages reusable logic with Vue's **Composition API**, the functions like `ref`, `computed` and `onMounted` you've been using. By convention it is named `useSomething`. It can create refs, computeds and watchers and register lifecycle hooks, which then belong to the component that called it.

```js
export function useMouse() {
  const x = ref(0), y = ref(0)
  const update = (e) => { x.value = e.pageX; y.value = e.pageY }
  onMounted(() => window.addEventListener('mousemove', update))
  onUnmounted(() => window.removeEventListener('mousemove', update))
  return { x, y }
}
```

Conventions that make composables pleasant to use:

- **Return a plain object of refs**, not a `reactive()`: callers can destructure (`const { x, y } = useMouse()`) without losing reactivity.
- **Accept refs, getters or plain values** as arguments and turn them into a plain value with `toValue()`. Read them inside a `watchEffect` or a watched getter so the composable reacts when the input changes.
- Call composables **at the top level of `<script setup>`** (like lifecycle hooks), so their hooks attach to the right component.
- Clean up what you set up (listeners, intervals, subscriptions).

Each call creates **independent state**. If you want state shared between components, create it outside the function, at the top level of the file, or use a Pinia store (next lessons).

Before writing one, check **VueUse**, a large collection of ready-made composables (`useLocalStorage`, `useFetch`, `useIntersectionObserver` and many more).
takeaways: A composable is a `useX()` function that bundles refs, computeds, watchers and hooks
Return an object of refs; accept refs/getters and read them with `toValue()`
Each call has its own state; state created outside the function, or Pinia, is shared
pitfalls: Returning `reactive({ x, y })` so callers lose reactivity when they destructure.

quiz.q: Two components each call `useCounter()`, which creates `const count = ref(0)` inside the function. Clicking + in one component...
options: Throws because the ref is shared
quiz.explain: Each call runs the function again and creates a separate ref; sharing needs module-level state or a store.

concepts.name: Provide / inject
concepts.summary: Pass data from an ancestor to any descendant without threading props through every level.
concepts.why: Themes, the current user, a form sharing its state with its inputs, and component libraries rely on provide/inject to avoid prop drilling.
concepts.body:
Passing a prop through five components that don't use it (**prop drilling**) is tedious. With **provide/inject**, an ancestor provides a value under a key and any descendant, however deep, injects it.

```js
// Ancestor
provide('theme', theme)          // theme is a ref
// Descendant
const theme = inject('theme', ref('light'))   // second arg = default
```

Key points:

- Provide **refs** (or reactive objects), not `.value`, so descendants see updates.
- Keep mutations with the provider: provide a read-only view with `readonly(theme)` plus a function like `setTheme`, so it is clear who changes the data.
- The nearest provider wins, so a subtree can override a value.
- `inject` without a default returns `undefined` (and warns) when no ancestor provides the key.
- `app.provide(key, value)` provides to the whole application; plugins use this.

For large apps, use **Symbol keys** (unique values made with `Symbol('theme')`, which can never clash), and with TypeScript type them as `InjectionKey<T>`: `export const ThemeKey: InjectionKey<Ref<string>> = Symbol('theme')`. Put keys in a shared module.

Provide/inject suits values that belong to one part of the page: a form providing its validation state to its inputs, a tabs component to its panels, the theme of a shared set of UI components. For app-wide state (cart, signed-in user) a Pinia store (coming up) is usually clearer and shows up in Vue DevTools.
takeaways: `provide(key, value)` in an ancestor, `inject(key, default)` in any descendant
Provide refs plus updater functions; wrap in `readonly` to keep mutations in one place
Use Symbol / `InjectionKey` keys in a shared module
pitfalls: Providing `count.value` instead of `count`, so descendants receive a plain copy that never updates.

quiz.q: A layout provides 'theme' and a nested section also provides 'theme'. What does a component inside the section inject?
quiz.explain: inject resolves the nearest ancestor that provides the key, so subtrees can override values.

concepts.name: Routing with Vue Router
concepts.summary: Show a different page component for each URL with Vue Router: routes, RouterView, RouterLink, parameters, loading on demand and guards.
concepts.why: Any app with several pages needs URLs that match what's showing, and Vue Router is the official tool.
concepts.body:
**Vue Router** maps URL paths to components; this job is called **routing**. You create a router with a history mode and a route table, install it with `app.use(router)`, and render the matched component with `<RouterView />`:

```js
const router = createRouter({
  history: createWebHistory(),
  routes: [
    { path: '/', component: Home },
    { path: '/users/:id', name: 'user', component: () => import('./UserPage.vue') },
  ],
})
```

- `createWebHistory()` gives clean URLs (the server must be set up to send `index.html` for paths it doesn't recognise); `createWebHashHistory()` uses `#/` URLs and needs no server config.
- `() => import(...)` downloads a page's code only when it's first visited (**code splitting**).
- **Dynamic segments** like `:id` appear in `useRoute().params.id`. The same component instance is reused when only params change, so watch `() => route.params.id` to reload data.
- **Nested routes** use `children` plus a `<RouterView />` inside the parent component.

Link to pages with `<RouterLink :to="{ name: 'user', params: { id: 7 } }">` (it adds active classes) or programmatically with `useRouter().push('/')`.

**Navigation guards** control access: `router.beforeEach((to) => { if (to.meta.requiresAuth && !isLoggedIn()) return { name: 'login' } })`. Return `false` to cancel, a route to send the user there instead, or nothing to continue. Per-component hooks like `onBeforeRouteLeave` help with "unsaved changes" warnings.
takeaways: Define routes, `app.use(router)`, render with `<RouterView>`
Load route components on demand with `() => import(...)`
Params are in `useRoute().params`; watch them when the same component is reused
Guards return false, a route to go to instead, or nothing
pitfalls: Fetching data only in `onMounted` of a route component; going from /users/1 to /users/2 reuses the component, so it keeps showing the old user's data.

quiz.q: Navigating from /users/1 to /users/2 with the same route component. What happens by default?
options: Nothing; the URL updates but params stay '1'
The component is destroyed and re-created
The same instance is reused; route.params.id changes
quiz.explain: Vue Router reuses the component when only params change, so code must react to route.params changes.

concepts.name: State management with Pinia
concepts.summary: Share application state across components with Pinia stores: state, getters, actions and storeToRefs.
concepts.why: Pinia is Vue's official store, used for anything many unrelated components need: the signed-in user, a cart, settings, cached data.
concepts.body:
When unrelated components need the same state, a **store** gives it one home. **Pinia** is the official choice. Install it with `app.use(createPinia())` and define stores with `defineStore`.

The **setup store** syntax will feel familiar because it is a composable:

```js
export const useCartStore = defineStore('cart', () => {
  const items = ref([])                         // state
  const total = computed(() => ...)             // getter
  function add(product) { items.value.push(product) }   // action
  return { items, total, add }
})
```

Every ref you return becomes state, computeds become getters and functions become actions. You must return all state so that tools can see it, such as **Vue DevTools**, a browser extension that shows your components and stores while you develop. (An "options store" with `state`, `getters` and `actions` keys also exists.)

In a component, call `const cart = useCartStore()`. The store is a reactive object, so access `cart.items` and `cart.total` without `.value`. All components share the same instance.

Destructuring a store loses reactivity. Use **`storeToRefs(cart)`** for state and getters; actions can be destructured directly.

Benefits over a plain `ref` at the top of a file: Vue DevTools can show and replay every change; edits update without losing state while you develop; and it has helpers (`$reset`, `$patch`, `$subscribe`) and plugins, for example to save state in `localStorage`.

Pinia is also safe with **server-side rendering (SSR)**, covered in a later lesson: the server builds each page's HTML before sending it, so visitors see content right away. The server loads your files once and then answers many visitors, so a `ref` at the top of a file would be shared by all of them; Pinia gives each request its own store.

Keep stores focused (one per area of the app: `useAuthStore`, `useCartStore`) and put async calls in actions.
takeaways: `defineStore('id', () => { ... return {...} })` defines a setup store
Returned refs = state, computeds = getters, functions = actions; return all state
Use `storeToRefs` when destructuring state and getters
pitfalls: `const { total } = useCartStore()` gives a value that never updates; use storeToRefs.

quiz.q: In an app using server-side rendering (the server builds each page's HTML), why use Pinia instead of exporting a ref from a file for shared state?
options: A ref at the top of a file is shared by every request the server handles, leaking one user's data to others; Pinia creates a store per request
Exported refs don't work with script setup
quiz.explain: The server loads each file once for all requests, so state created at the top of a file is shared across users; Pinia ties stores to each app instance.

concepts.name: Vue with TypeScript
concepts.summary: Type props, emits, models, refs, template refs, provide/inject and generic components, and check templates with vue-tsc.
concepts.why: Most professional Vue code is TypeScript; knowing the typed APIs prevents many bugs that would otherwise only show up while the app runs.
concepts.body:
Vue 3 is written in TypeScript and `<script setup lang="ts">` gives first-class typing. Templates are checked by **`vue-tsc`**, a **type checker** (the tool that reads type labels and reports mistakes) that understands `.vue` files; teams often run `vue-tsc --noEmit` automatically on every change. The Vue language tools do the same in your editor.

The main typed APIs:

- **Props**: `defineProps<{ title: string; size?: 'sm' | 'lg' }>()`. With 3.5 destructuring, defaults are plain JavaScript: `const { size = 'sm' } = defineProps<...>()`.
- **Emits**: `defineEmits<{ select: [id: number]; close: [] }>()` types each event's arguments.
- **Models**: `defineModel<string>()` or `defineModel<number>({ required: true })`.
- **Refs**: TypeScript usually works out the type itself; annotate when the initial value is narrower than later values: `ref<User | null>(null)`.
- **Template refs**: `useTemplateRef<HTMLInputElement>('input')`; recent tooling works it out from the template automatically.
- **Provide/inject**: `InjectionKey<T>` keys make `inject` return `T | undefined`.

**Generic** components take a type parameter, a placeholder type like `T` that each use fills in, on the `<script>` tag: `<script setup lang="ts" generic="T extends { id: string }">`. Then `defineProps<{ items: T[] }>()` and slot or emit types can reference `T`, and the parent's usage is checked against the `T` worked out from what it passes.

Type-only imports in `defineProps` work for interfaces from other files. Keep prop types to simple object types: Vue's build step must read them to produce the prop checks that run in the browser.
concepts.code:
<script setup lang="ts" generic="T extends { id: number }">
import { ref, computed, useTemplateRef, onMounted } from 'vue'

const { items, max = 10 } = defineProps<{ items: T[]; max?: number }>()
const emit = defineEmits<{ select: [item: T]; clear: [] }>()
const query = defineModel<string>('query', { default: '' })

const selected = ref<T | null>(null)
const shown = computed(() => items.slice(0, max))
const search = useTemplateRef<HTMLInputElement>('search')
onMounted(() => search.value?.focus())

function pick(item: T) {
  selected.value = item
  emit('select', item)        // emit('select', 42) would be a type error
}
</script>

<template>
  <input ref="search" v-model="query">
  <slot v-for="item in shown" :key="item.id" :item="item" :pick="pick" />
</template>
takeaways: `defineProps<T>()`, `defineEmits<{ e: [args] }>()`, `defineModel<T>()`
Annotate refs whose type widens: `ref<User | null>(null)`
`generic="T"` on the script tag creates generic components
Run `vue-tsc --noEmit` to type-check templates
pitfalls: Relying on `tsc` alone; it ignores `.vue` files and templates, so use `vue-tsc`.

quiz.q: Which command type-checks .vue files including their templates?
quiz.explain: Plain tsc doesn't understand SFCs; vue-tsc wraps it with Vue's language tooling.

concepts.name: Transition, Teleport and KeepAlive
concepts.summary: Animate entering and leaving elements, render modals outside the component tree and cache inactive components.
concepts.why: These built-ins solve common UI problems (animations, modals, preserving tab state) that are tricky to hand-roll.
concepts.body:
Vue ships several built-in components.

**`<Transition>`** animates a single element or component that is inserted or removed by `v-if`, `v-show`, a dynamic component or a key change. It adds classes at the right moments: with `name="fade"` you style `fade-enter-from`, `fade-enter-active`, `fade-leave-to` and `fade-leave-active`. `mode="out-in"` waits for the old element to leave before the new one enters. JavaScript hooks (`@enter`, `@leave`) let you use an animation library. **`<TransitionGroup>`** animates items in a `v-for` list, including moves via the `*-move` class; items need keys.

**`<Teleport to="body">`** renders its content elsewhere in the DOM while it still behaves as part of the component (props, events and provide/inject still work). Use it for pop-up dialogs, notifications and tooltips that must appear above everything, even when a parent element would cut them off. `:disabled` keeps the content in place, and Vue 3.5's `defer` prop lets the target be an element that appears later in the same update.

**`<KeepAlive>`** caches component instances instead of destroying them when they are switched out, typically around `<component :is="tab">` (which shows whichever component `tab` holds) or `<RouterView>`'s slot. State and scroll positions survive tab switches. Limit it with `include`, `exclude` and `max`. Cached components get `onActivated` and `onDeactivated` hooks instead of mount/unmount on each switch.

**`<Suspense>`** shows a fallback while components that load asynchronously aren't ready yet; it is still marked experimental.
takeaways: `<Transition name="x">` adds x-enter-from / x-leave-to etc. classes around v-if/v-show
`<Teleport to="body">` moves DOM output but keeps component relationships
`<KeepAlive>` caches switched-out components; use `onActivated`/`onDeactivated`
pitfalls: Wrapping several root elements in `<Transition>`; it animates one element, use `<TransitionGroup>` for lists.

quiz.q: A modal inside a card with overflow: hidden gets clipped. Which built-in fixes it while keeping the modal's props and events working?
quiz.explain: Teleport renders the modal's DOM under another target (like body) while it stays a child in the component tree.

concepts.name: Advanced reactivity APIs
concepts.summary: Control reactivity precisely with shallowRef, triggerRef, markRaw, toRaw, readonly, customRef and effectScope.
concepts.why: Very large data, objects from other libraries and library code need finer control than ref and reactive give by default.
concepts.body:
Default reactivity is **deep**: every nested object is wrapped in a Proxy on access. That is convenient but has costs for large or foreign data. The advanced APIs give you control.

- **`shallowRef(value)`** tracks only `.value` assignment, not nested changes. Ideal for large immutable data (replace it wholesale: `rows.value = newRows`) and for holding component definitions or class instances. After mutating inside one, call **`triggerRef(r)`** to force an update.
- **`shallowReactive(obj)`** makes only top-level properties reactive.
- **`markRaw(obj)`** flags an object so Vue never wraps it in a proxy: map and chart objects, or clients from other libraries.
- **`toRaw(proxy)`** returns the original object, useful for passing to libraries, `structuredClone`, or comparing identity.
- **`readonly(x)`** gives a deep read-only proxy that warns on mutation.
- **`customRef((track, trigger) => ({ get, set }))`** builds a ref with custom timing, such as one that only updates once changes pause.
- **`effectScope()`** groups the **effects** (watchers and computeds) created inside `scope.run(() => ...)` so `scope.stop()` disposes them all at once. It is how libraries create state shared by many components outside any one of them.

Identity gotcha: `reactive(obj) !== obj`. Mutating the raw object bypasses tracking, and storing the raw object in a Set then searching for the proxy fails. Always work through the proxy (or consistently through the raw object with markRaw).
takeaways: `shallowRef` + replacement for large or external data; `triggerRef` after in-place edits
`markRaw` keeps class instances and library objects out of the proxy system
`effectScope` collects effects so they can be stopped together
pitfalls: Comparing a reactive proxy with the raw object by identity (`===`), or mixing both in Sets and Maps.

quiz.q: You store a 3D-engine scene object in a ref and the app becomes slow. What is the most likely fix?
options: Wrap it with markRaw() or hold it in a shallowRef
quiz.explain: Deep reactivity proxies every nested property of the huge object; markRaw or shallowRef avoids that.

concepts.name: Custom directives and plugins
concepts.summary: Package low-level page behaviour in custom directives, and app-wide features as plugins.
concepts.why: Directives and plugins are how you extend Vue itself, and how most Vue libraries are installed.
concepts.body:
Composables reuse logic built on state; **custom directives** reuse low-level DOM manipulation on plain elements. A directive is an object of lifecycle hooks: `created`, `beforeMount`, `mounted`, `beforeUpdate`, `updated`, `beforeUnmount`, `unmounted`. Each receives the element, a `binding` object and a third argument you rarely need, where `binding.value` is the expression's value, `binding.arg` is the argument (`v-tooltip:top` gives `'top'`) and `binding.modifiers` is an object of modifiers.

In `<script setup>`, any camelCase variable starting with `v` is usable as a directive: `const vFocus = { mounted: (el) => el.focus() }` enables `<input v-focus>`. A function shorthand runs on both `mounted` and `updated`. Register globally with `app.directive('focus', vFocus)`.

Prefer components or composables when possible; directives are for things like focus, click-outside, noticing when an element scrolls into view, and tooltips. They don't work well on components with more than one top-level element.

A **plugin** is an object with `install(app, options)` (or just a function). Inside it you can:

- register components and directives with `app.component` / `app.directive`,
- make values available with `app.provide(key, value)`,
- add `app.config.globalProperties.$x` for template access (use sparingly),
- set `app.config.errorHandler` or other app config.

Users install it with `app.use(plugin, options)`. Vue Router, Pinia and translation (i18n) libraries are all plugins.
takeaways: Directives are objects of hooks receiving `(el, binding)`; use them for DOM-level behaviour
In `<script setup>`, `vSomething` variables are directives automatically
A plugin is `install(app, options)`; it registers components, directives and provides
pitfalls: Forgetting to remove listeners in `unmounted`, leaking handlers for every mounted element.

quiz.q:
What is `binding.arg` for `

`?
quiz.explain: The part after the colon is the argument; modifiers come after dots and the value is the expression.

concepts.name: Performance optimisation
concepts.summary: Find and fix slow Vue apps: loading code on demand, stable props, v-once and v-memo, shallow state and list virtualization.
concepts.why: Vue is fast by default, but large lists, heavy components and careless props can still make apps sluggish.
concepts.body:
Measure first: the Vue devtools performance timeline and the browser's performance profiler (a tool that measures where time goes) show which components render often or slowly. Then apply the matching fix.

**Load less**: load the code of routes and heavy components only when needed with `defineAsyncComponent(() => import('./Chart.vue'))`; check how big your JavaScript files are; import only what you use from big libraries.

**Update less**:

- **Props stability**: a child re-renders when any prop it receives changes. Passing `:active-id="activeId"` to every row re-renders all rows on each change; passing `:active="item.id === activeId"` re-renders only the two affected rows.
- **`v-once`** renders a subtree once and skips it forever after.
- **`v-memo="[item.selected]"`** skips updating a subtree (often a `v-for` row) unless the listed values change.
- **Computed stability**: since 3.4 computeds trigger only when their value changes, but returning a new object each time defeats that; compare manually if needed.

**Track less**: deep reactivity over huge arrays costs memory and time. Use `shallowRef` for large data you replace wholesale and `markRaw` for non-UI objects.

**Render less**: lists with thousands of rows should use **list virtualization** (render only the visible rows) with a library such as vue-virtual-scroller or TanStack Virtual. Don't wrap every tiny piece of a huge list in its own component; each component instance costs some extra work.

The production build (what you publish) drops development warnings and is much faster than development mode; always measure that.
takeaways: Profile in production mode before optimising
Keep props stable: pass derived booleans, not shared ids, to list rows
`v-once`, `v-memo`, `shallowRef`, async components and list virtualization cover most hot spots
pitfalls: Using `v-memo` with an incomplete list of values, so rows don't update when other data changes.

quiz.q: Every row receives :selected-id="selectedId" and compares it internally. Selecting a new row re-renders...
options: Only the old and new selected rows
Every row, because each row's prop changed
quiz.explain: Each row's selectedId prop changes, so all rows update; passing a per-row boolean limits updates to two rows.

concepts.name: How reactivity works inside
concepts.summary: Understand Vue's Proxy-based tracking: track and trigger, effects and subscribers, the scheduler and the 3.5 version-counting redesign.
concepts.why: Knowing the mechanism explains every reactivity gotcha and is essential when writing libraries or tracking down rare bugs.
concepts.body:
Vue's reactivity is a map, built while the app runs, of which code depends on which data. It is made from **proxies** and refs with getters and setters.

`reactive(obj)` returns a Proxy whose `get` trap calls **track** (record that the currently running effect depends on `target.key`) and returns the value, lazily wrapping nested objects in proxies. The `set` and `deleteProperty` traps call **trigger**, which notifies every subscriber of that key. Array methods like `push` and iteration are handled specially (iteration tracks an internal key, length changes trigger it). A `ref` is an object whose `value` getter and setter do the same tracking for one value.

An **effect** is a function run while it is the "active subscriber", so every reactive read it performs subscribes it. Component render functions, `computed` and `watch` are all built on this. Dependencies are recollected on every run, which is why branches not taken don't subscribe.

Vue 3.5 rewrote the internals: each dependency keeps a **version** counter and subscribers are connected to their dependencies through linked lists (chains of objects that point to each other) instead of Sets. A computed is lazy and only recomputes if a dependency's version changed since it last ran, which made computeds cheaper and reduced memory use substantially.

Triggered component updates don't run immediately: they are queued as jobs in a **scheduler** (Vue's to-do list of pending updates), with duplicates dropped, sorted parent-first and flushed in a microtask. `nextTick()` returns that flush's promise. Watchers default to the `pre` flush (before component updates), `post` runs after, and `sync` runs immediately on every change.

Reads outside an effect, through `toRaw`, or after an `await` in an effect are not tracked.
takeaways: Proxy `get` tracks the running effect; `set` triggers subscribers of that key
Renders, computeds and watchers are all effects; dependencies are recollected each run
Component updates are batched by a scheduler and flushed in a microtask (`nextTick`)
3.5 uses per-dependency versions so computeds recompute only when needed
pitfalls: Expecting reads after an `await` inside `watchEffect` to be tracked; only the part before the first `await` is.

quiz.q: Inside watchEffect, code reads a.value, then awaits a fetch, then reads b.value. Changing b later...
options: Does not re-run it, because b was read after the await when no effect was active
quiz.explain: Tracking only happens while the effect runs synchronously; after the await the active subscriber is gone.

quiz.q: Why does `state.count++` three times in one handler cause only one re-render?
options: Only the last set trap runs
Update jobs are queued, deduplicated and flushed once in a microtask
quiz.explain: Trigger schedules the component's update job; the scheduler dedupes it and runs it once at the next flush.

concepts.name: Compiler, virtual DOM and render functions
concepts.summary: See how templates become render functions with patch flags, block trees and cached static parts, and when to write render functions yourself.
concepts.why: Understanding what Vue's build step does to templates explains its speed, and lets you write render functions for very dynamic components.
concepts.body:
Vue uses a **virtual DOM**: a **render function** returns a tree of lightweight objects (vnodes) describing the page, and Vue **patches** the real DOM by comparing the new tree with the previous one. Vue's twist: templates have a fixed structure, so its **compiler** (the build step that turns templates into render functions) adds hints that let Vue skip most of that comparing.

- **Static hoisting / caching**: fully static elements are created once and reused across renders.
- **Patch flags**: each dynamic vnode carries a number whose bits say what can change (`TEXT`, `CLASS`, `PROPS` with a list of prop names...), so patching checks only those.
- **Block tree**: a block (a template root, or the inside of a `v-if`/`v-for`) collects its dynamic descendants into a flat `dynamicChildren` array. Updates walk that array instead of the whole subtree, so the cost scales with dynamic nodes, not template size.

You can see the output in the Vue SFC Playground's JS tab.

Hand-written **render functions** use `h(type, props, children)`, or JSX (HTML-like tags inside JavaScript) via a plugin. Use them for components whose structure is very dynamic (e.g. a heading level from a prop, or components that generate markup from data), and in libraries. They lose compiler optimisations and are harder to read, so templates remain the default. A `<script setup>` component can't return a render function, but `setup()` in `defineComponent` can.

Vue's upcoming **Vapor mode** compiles templates directly to DOM operations without a virtual DOM, for opt-in components.
takeaways: Templates compile to render functions returning vnodes; the runtime patches the DOM
Patch flags, block trees and static caching let updates skip static parts
`h(type, props, children)` render functions suit highly dynamic components
pitfalls: Rewriting ordinary components as render functions for speed; templates are usually faster thanks to compiler hints.

quiz.q: Why does a mostly static 500-line template update quickly when only one text binding changes?
options: The block tree's dynamicChildren lists only the dynamic nodes, and patch flags limit checks to the text
quiz.explain: The compiler records the dynamic nodes and what can change on them, so patching visits only that span's text.

concepts.name: SSR, hydration and Nuxt
concepts.summary: Render Vue on the server, hydrate it in the browser, avoid hydration mismatches and know what Nuxt adds.
concepts.why: Server rendering shows content sooner and lets search engines read pages, but brings state-leak and mismatch bugs that need expert understanding.
concepts.body:
With **server-side rendering**, the server runs your components to produce HTML, the browser shows it immediately, and then Vue **hydrates** it: it creates the same app with `createSSRApp`, walks the existing DOM instead of creating it, and attaches listeners and reactivity.

On the server you call `renderToString(app)` (or a variant that sends the HTML in pieces as it's ready) from `vue/server-renderer`. Only `setup` and server-safe code run; `onMounted` and other DOM hooks do not, so browser-only code belongs there.

Two classes of bugs dominate:

- **Cross-request state pollution**: the server program loads each module once and keeps running, so refs or stores created at the top of a file are shared by all users. Create the app, router and Pinia **per request**.
- **Hydration mismatches**: if the client's first render differs from the server HTML (dates, `Math.random()`, `window` checks, invalid HTML nesting like a `div` inside a `p`), Vue warns and fixes the page up. Fix the cause: render such values only after mount, or mark an intentional difference with Vue 3.5's `data-allow-mismatch` attribute. Use `useId()` for ids that must match on both sides.

Vue 3.5 adds **lazy hydration** for async components: `defineAsyncComponent({ loader, hydrate: hydrateOnVisible() })` delays hydrating parts further down the page that aren't visible yet (also `hydrateOnIdle`, `hydrateOnInteraction`, `hydrateOnMediaQuery`).

Hand-rolled SSR is rare. **Nuxt**, a framework built on Vue, provides server rendering, pages built ahead of time, pages defined by files in a folder, data loading (`useFetch`, `useAsyncData`) that hands server-loaded data to the browser, and server API code. Learning raw SSR mainly helps you debug Nuxt.
takeaways: SSR renders HTML on the server; hydration attaches Vue to it with `createSSRApp`
Create app, router and stores per request to avoid leaking state between users
Mismatches come from output that differs between runs (times, random numbers) or browser-only values; fix or mark them
Nuxt bundles SSR, routing and data loading for real projects
pitfalls: Rendering `new Date().toLocaleTimeString()` during SSR; the client renders a different time and hydration mismatches.

quiz.q: A store defined as a module-level reactive object is used in an SSR app. What is the risk?
options: The store won't be reactive on the client
None, modules are re-evaluated per request
State from one user's request can leak into another user's render
quiz.explain: Server modules are evaluated once and shared by all requests, so module-level state is shared across users.
